posts.text: “Everything is easy when you are busy. But nothing is easy when you are lazy.” I read this line, often said to be from Swami Vivekananda, and I kept thinking about it. At first it sounds like simple advice to keep working. But the more I thought about it, the more I felt it is about what my mind does when I give it nothing to do. Here is what I learned from it. When I am busy with useful work When I am busy with work that matters, my mind has something real to focus on: tasks to finish, problems to solve, things to build. This keeps me in the present. When I am busy, I spend far less time going round in circles about: what happened in the past, and what I could have done differently what might happen in the future, and what could go wrong what other people said, meant or might be thinking things I cannot control, no matter how much I think about them Being busy does not mean I will never overthink. But useful work gives my mind a clear direction . When I have too much free time When I have nothing interesting to do, my mind starts going back to old situations or worrying about problems that have not happened yet. Thinking is not bad. Looking back helps me learn, and planning helps me prepare. The problem starts when I keep thinking the same thoughts again and again, and it leads to nothing useful. For example, I might keep thinking about something that happened yesterday, get angry about it again, and then be impatient with my family or friends who had nothing to do with it. I may not have been able to control what happened. But I could control how I reacted , and my reaction created a new problem, for me and for the people around me. What this quote means to me For me, this quote is not about being busy every minute of the day. It is about using my mind in a good way. I see two very different ways I can spend my time. Using my mind well Focusing on something useful, accepting what I cannot change, and dealing calmly with what is happening right now. Getting stuck in my thoughts Going back to the past again and again, worrying about a future nobody can predict, and letting that anger come out on the people around me. Being busy is not always the answer Staying busy does not fix everything. Sometimes what I need is rest, some quiet time, or time to understand how I feel. The goal is not to run away from my thoughts by staying busy all the time. It is to stop getting stuck in thoughts that do not help me. What I am taking from this I cannot control everything that happens around me. But I can choose what I focus on, how I react, and how I treat the people around me. Understanding my own thoughts a little better makes life a little easier, not just for me, but for the people around me too.

This is one of the most common questions in a Salesforce developer interview. Most people answer "governor limits" and stop there. A strong answer explains what actually breaks, shows the fix, and shows how you would prove the fix works. The question "Why is it a bad practice to write a SOQL query or a DML statement inside a for loop?" The short answer Salesforce limits how much work one transaction can do. In normal (synchronous) code you get 100 SOQL queries and 150 DML statements . A trigger can receive up to 200 records at a time. If your code runs one query per record, 200 records means 200 queries, and the whole transaction fails. The error you will see When the code goes over the limit, Salesforce stops it and rolls back everything it did. The error looks like this: System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries: 101 For DML inside a loop, the message is Too many DML statements: 151 . A limit error cannot be caught with try and catch, so the only real fix is to change the code. Code that breaks This trigger copies an account's phone number to all of its contacts: trigger AccountTrigger on Account (after update) { for (Account acc : Trigger.new) { List<Contact> contacts = [SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE AccountId = :acc.Id]; for (Contact c : contacts) { c.Phone = acc.Phone; update c; } } } It works when you test it with one account. It fails when a data load updates 200 accounts, because the query runs 200 times, and the update runs once for every single contact. The fix Run one query for all the accounts, change the contacts in memory, and save them all with one update. Trigger.newMap gives each account by its Id, so every contact can find its own account without another query. trigger AccountTrigger on Account (after update) { List<Contact> contacts = [SELECT Id, AccountId FROM Contact WHERE AccountId IN :Trigger.newMap.keySet()]; for (Contact c : contacts) { c.Phone = Trigger.newMap.get(c.AccountId).Phone; } update contacts; } Now the code uses one query and one DML statement , whether it receives 1 account or 200. Other limits worth knowing 200 SOQL queries in asynchronous code (Batch, Queueable, future methods), instead of 100 50,000 records in total can be returned by all queries in one transaction 10,000 records in total can be changed by DML in one transaction 150 DML statements , in both synchronous and asynchronous code How to prove your code is safe Write a test that sends 200 records at once, the same as a real data load: @isTest private class AccountTriggerTest { @isTest static void updatesTwoHundredAccounts() { List<Account> accounts = new List<Account>(); for (Integer i = 0; i < 200; i++) { accounts.add(new Account(Name = 'Test ' + i)); } insert accounts; List<Contact> contacts = new List<Contact>(); for (Account acc : accounts) { contacts.add(new Contact(LastName = 'Test', AccountId = acc.Id)); } insert contacts; for (Account acc : accounts) { acc.Phone = '9999999999'; } Test.startTest(); update accounts; Test.stopTest(); Assert.areEqual(200, [SELECT COUNT() FROM Contact WHERE Phone = '9999999999']); } } If the trigger had a query inside the loop, this test would fail with the limit error. You can also see how many queries your code has used at any point: System.debug(Limits.getQueries() + ' of ' + Limits.getLimitQueries() + ' queries used'); What the interviewer wants to hear You know the limits are per transaction, not per record. You always write code for many records, not for one. You know the pattern: collect the Ids, query once, change in memory, update once. You test with 200 records to prove it. Follow-up questions to expect What if I need the related records for each parent? Use a subquery, so one query brings each account together with its contacts: List<Contact> contactsToUpdate = new List<Contact>(); for (Account acc : [SELECT Id, Phone, (SELECT Id FROM Contacts) FROM Account WHERE Id IN :Trigger.newMap.keySet()]) { for (Contact c : acc.Contacts) { c.Phone = acc.Phone; contactsToUpdate.add(c); } } update contactsToUpdate; Or run one query and group the results in a Map<Id, List<Contact>> , with the account Id as the key. Can I read the account's phone in the same query? Yes. Query the contacts and include Account.Phone , the parent's field. Each contact then carries its account's phone, so you do not need a map at all: List<Contact> contactsToUpdate = new List<Contact>(); for (Contact con : [SELECT Id, Phone, Account.Phone FROM Contact WHERE AccountId IN :Trigger.newMap.keySet()]) { con.Phone = con.Account.Phone; contactsToUpdate.add(con); } update contactsToUpdate; This works in an after update trigger, because by then the query already sees the account's new phone number. Can I avoid the limit by catching the error? No. A LimitException cannot be caught. The code has to be written so it never reaches the limit. Does the same rule apply to Flows? Yes. A Get Records, Create Records or Update Records element inside a Flow loop counts against the same limits. Move it outside the loop: collect the records in a collection variable inside the loop, then save them with one element after it.
